stories.headline: Cyclone Murasu nears Andhra, Odisha days after Arnab; Chennai schools shut
stories.title: Cyclone Murasu nears Andhra, Odisha days after Arnab; Chennai schools shut
stories.summary: Cyclone Murasu nears Andhra, Odisha days after Arnab; Chennai schools shut
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Cyclone Murasu is approaching the Andhra Pradesh coast as authorities evacuate vulnerable residents.
The fresh threat has complicated ongoing relief operations after Cyclone Arnab.
Less than a week after Cyclone Arnab struck Andhra Pradesh, the state and neighbouring Odisha are preparing for another cyclone while relief and restoration work continues.
Cyclone Murasu is expected to cross the Andhra coast near Ongole late Monday night or early Tuesday, with winds of 100–110 kmph, gusting to 120 kmph.
Andhra Pradesh has deployed disaster response teams and ordered evacuations from unsafe areas.
Odisha is moving residents from low-lying settlements and landslide-prone hillsides, while Chennai has declared a school holiday on November 2 as heavy to very heavy rain is forecast.
The fresh threat comes as around 1.18 lakh people in Odisha remain affected by the floods and landslides following Arnab’s landfall on October 28.
Further rain in southern Odisha through November 4 could hamper recovery efforts and trigger fresh flooding and landslides.
Murasu intensified into a cyclonic storm over the Bay of Bengal on Sunday.

According to the India Meteorological Department’s (IMD) 5.30 pm update, it was about 420 kilometres east-southeast of Chennai and 490 kilometres east-southeast of Nellore, moving west-northwestwards at 25 kmph.
It is expected to strengthen into a severe cyclonic storm by the early hours of November 2 before turning northwestwards towards Andhra Pradesh.
The latest forecast places landfall between Nellore and Narsapur, close to Ongole in Prakasam district, between 11.30 pm on November 2 and 4 am on November 3.

stories.headline: A.P. seeks assistance from Tamil Nadu, Karnataka for cyclone power restoration
stories.title: A.P. seeks assistance from Tamil Nadu, Karnataka for cyclone power restoration
reasons: source: event has 2 copies, primary source counted once
corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Anticipating the possibility of large-scale damage to electricity infrastructure, particularly the uprooting of electric poles in cyclone-affected areas, Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu on Sunday spoke with Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Vijay and Karnataka Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar.
Naidu requested them to send necessary personnel and machinery to Andhra Pradesh to undertake electricity infrastructure restoration works in the wake of the cyclone.
Both Chief Ministers responded positively and assured they would extend all possible assistance to Andhra Pradesh.
Chandrababu Naidu said AP officials would coordinate with their counterparts in the two states to facilitate the required support.
Meanwhile, personnel from Telangana are already engaged in field-level operations to restore the electricity infrastructure damaged by Cyclone Arnab.

As a precautionary measure, the Andhra Pradesh Government has also kept electricity department personnel who have completed restoration work in Cyclone Arnab-affected areas ready for deployment in regions likely to be affected by Cyclone Murasu, the release added.

stories.headline: Cyclone Arnab toll rises to 6 in Odisha, search on for 10 missing
stories.title: Cyclone Arnab toll rises to 6 in Odisha, search on for 10 missing
stories.summary: Cyclone Arnab toll rises to 6 in Odisha, search on for 10 missing
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Rescuers recovered two bodies and continued searching for 10 missing villagers in Gidipabali.
The disaster underscores the deadly landslide and flood risks following Cyclone Arnab.

The death toll from incidents linked to Cyclone Arnab in Odisha rose to six on Sunday after rescue teams recovered two bodies from a landslide-hit village on the border of Ganjam and Kandhamal districts.
Ten people remain missing as teams search through mud, boulders and debris.
Heavy rain triggered by the cyclone sent sludge and rocks crashing down the hills in Gidipabali, levelling houses while residents slept.
At least 13 people who escaped have been sheltered at a relief centre near G Udaygiri, Kandhamal District Collector Vedbhusan said.
Odisha has reported around 10 landslides following incessant rain brought by the cyclone, which made landfall in neighbouring Andhra Pradesh on October 28.
Rinima Mallik, who survived the landslide, walked 25 kilometres along forest roads with her two children on her shoulders to reach the relief centre near G Udaygiri.
Her husband and father remain missing.
“My husband and father are missing.
How to support my twins?
We do not want to go back to the village,” she said, urging the government to help her settle elsewhere.

stories.headline: Cyclone-hit Godavari region records steady high voter turnout
stories.title: Cyclone-hit Godavari region records steady high voter turnout
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The election to the 14 Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), including three nagar panchayats, on Sunday witnessed a commendable voter turnout across the Godavari region despite them being busy recovering from the devastation caused by ‘Cyclone Arnab’.
Among all the ULBs, Narsapuram and Amalapuram municipalities were among the worst-hit by the cyclone, but voters thronged polling stations to exercise their franchise.
Simultaneously, relief operations of ‘Cyclone Arnab’ continued in the two towns of Narsapuram and Amalapuram.
In Amalapuram municipality at least 71.87 % voters exercised their vote.
In Narsapuram municipality, the area where the cyclone made its landfall on October 29, 70% voters cast their vote.
In Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema district, Ramachandrapuram municipality witnessed a turnout of 70.73%, while Mummudivaram nagar panchayat registered 75.09%.
Pawan’s own turf: In Kakinada district, the total polling percentage was 68.42.
In Pithapuram assembly constituency, represented by Deputy Chief Minister K. Pawan Kalyan, Pithapuram and Gollaprolu municipalities witnessed polling percentages of 66.31 and 74.36, respectively.
In the upland areas of Kakinada district, Peddapuram registered 66.86% polling while Samarlakota and Tuni recorded 70.57 % and 65.24 % respectively.
In Yeleswaram nagar panchayat, which recorded a turnout of 71.40%, polling was halted for some time due to technical glitches.
Voters pointed out the absence of the BJP candidate’s name and symbol on the ballot papers given to at one polling station.
At another polling station, the name and symbol of a TDP candidate were reportedly missing from the ballot papers.

stories.headline: Cyclone Murasu | Paddy farmers in Telangana fear crop damage amid high market prices
stories.title: Cyclone Murasu | Paddy farmers in Telangana fear crop damage amid high market prices
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The rain forecast under the impact of cyclonic storm Murasu (war drum) in various districts of Telangana from Monday to Wednesday (November 2 to 4) is giving jitters to farmers whose paddy and cotton crops are in various stages of cultivation.
According to farmers, when rice panicles get soaked in rain and droops, machines used for harvesting paddy have to be hired for some more time, which results in spending more money.
The soaked produce has to be dried, which may result in loss of some weight.
Labour also need to be hired to channel water away from damaged paddy crops.
And those in the pre-flowering stage might suffer greater damage.
Currently, paddy crops are in various stages — depending on the time of sowing — ranging from harvest, nearing harvest and pre-flowering stage.

The cyclonic storm is posing a threat to farmers at a time when they are getting relatively more prices for harvest — ranging from ₹3,500 to ₹4,500 per quintal of fresh produce, against around ₹2,900 (MSP and ₹500 bonus for fine rice) of dried crop earlier.
Cotton crops, which are nearing harvest, may suffer similar damage.

Sankranthi Narasiah, a paddy farmer from Lalapuram village, Konijerla mandal, Khammam, said that his and other crops around him are in various stages — ranging from pre-flowering to panicle formation.
“Wind and rain in this stage will cause us great loss,” said Mr. Narsaiah.
Khammam is one of the six districts forecast to receive heavy to very heavy rainfall on Monday (November 2, 2026).
Mahabubnagar, Nalgonda, Suryapet, Nagarkurnool and Wanaparthy are the remaining five.

stories.headline: Cyclone Murasu approaches Andhra coast; Odisha, Tamil Nadu issue alerts
stories.title: Cyclone Murasu approaches Andhra coast; Odisha, Tamil Nadu issue alerts
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast wind speeds of 100–110 kmph, gusting up to 120 kmph, during landfall.
The system is expected to intensify into a severe cyclonic storm before crossing the coast.

Amaravati/Bhubaneswar/Chennai: Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and Tamil Nadu have stepped up precautionary measures as Cyclone Murasu intensified over the Bay of Bengal and is expected to cross the south Andhra Pradesh coast between Nellore and Narsapur during the night of November 2 and the early hours of November 3.
The approaching storm has prompted Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu to direct officials to remain prepared for rescue and relief operations.
Odisha has sounded a high alert in its southern districts, while Tamil Nadu has asked district collectors to remain vigilant in view of the forecast of heavy to very heavy rainfall.
Naidu on Sunday directed officials to ensure that adequate personnel and equipment were available for rescue and relief operations in vulnerable areas.
He also asked them to prepare timelines for restoring electricity in the event of damage to power infrastructure and communicate the information to the public.

"Another cyclone is approaching Andhra Pradesh and officials must remain fully prepared to undertake relief and rescue operations, as a severe cyclonic storm is expected to cross the coast near Bapatla on the morning of November 3," said Naidu in an official press release.
Officials told the Chief Minister that the system was expected to intensify into a cyclonic storm and subsequently strengthen into a severe cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal.
Several coastal districts are likely to receive moderate to heavy rainfall on November 2, with isolated extremely heavy showers.
Heavy to very heavy rainfall is forecast in parts of the state on November 3 and 4.
Eluru, Krishna, NTR, West Godavari, Guntur and Bapatla are among the districts expected to receive significant rainfall.

stories.headline: US midterms: How Trump’s noncitizen voter lists could affect election results
stories.title: US midterms: How Trump’s noncitizen voter lists could affect election results
stories.summary: With Republicans fighting to retain control of Congress, the administration’s voter eligibility drive has raised questions over election challenges
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'election results' in title weight 64
article_sentences: As Americans head to the polls on Tuesday for midterm elections, lists the Trump administration has compiled of possible noncitizen voters could be used to contest the validity of the results.
With US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party fighting to maintain control of Congress, here’s how the lists could affect the midterms.

The Trump administration has acknowledged sending letters to election officials in five states — California, Washington, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Nevada — as of October 30, saying it identified noncitizens on their voter rolls, according to a Justice Department document seen by Reuters.

In an October 13 letter, the Justice Department demanded California not count ballots from about 20,000 registered voters "who federal agencies reasonably believe are likely noncitizens" without first verifying their citizenship, warning that election workers who processed them could face prosecution.
Trump endorsed the warning on social media: “They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!”
Noncitizen voting is illegal and can lead to jail time, fines and deportation.
The White House says noncitizen voting is a significant problem requiring aggressive enforcement to protect election integrity.
Trump has long alleged it is widespread, but available evidence indicates it is exceedingly rare.

A Reuters investigation in July found just 129 cases in which noncitizens were federally charged with voting illegally since a federal “voting by aliens” statute was created by Congress in 1996; many appeared to stem from confusion or administrative errors rather than intentional fraud.
The Justice Department has since ramped up noncitizens voting prosecutions.
“Close elections are not rare, and every illegal ballot cancels out the vote of an American citizen,” a Justice Department spokesperson, Kiersten Pels, said in a statement.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin claimed without evidence in a Fox News interview on Saturday that his agency had found 300,000 noncitizens on the voter rolls.

stories.headline: J&K Draft Mountain Policy proposes visitor limits at tourist hotspots to check overcrowding
stories.title: J&K Draft Mountain Policy proposes visitor limits at tourist hotspots to check overcrowding
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 1: A draft policy on sustainable mountain development has proposed a major overhaul of tourism management, infrastructure development and environmental protection in Jammu and Kashmir, including daily visitor limits at popular destinations, restrictions on private vehicles, a green cess of up to Rs 2,000 for foreign tourists and tighter controls on construction in ecologically sensitive areas. The Draft Jammu and Kashmir Sustainable Mountain Development Policy (JK-SMDP 2026), dated October 12, 2026, envisages a framework to regulate tourism, protect fragile mountain ecosystems and ensure that local communities benefit from economic activity in the region. The document, which is still a draft for consideration, does not represent an approved government decision. Its recommendations would require formal approval and, where necessary, legal backing before they could be implemented. One of its key proposals is to introduce carrying-capacity limits at 15 high-pressure tourist destinations, including Gulmarg, Pahalgam, Sonamarg, Doodhpathri, Yusmarg, Gurez, Bangus, Sinthan Top, Patnitop, Katra, Paddar, Basoli and Bhaderwah. The draft proposes that scientific carrying-capacity studies be completed within 12 months. Pending these studies, interim daily visitor limits could be introduced within 100 days of the proposed policy’s approval, based on the capacity of roads, parking facilities and sanitation infrastructure. It also envisages an online registration and time-slot booking system for visitors at high-pressure destinations, supported by digital entry passes, cess collection, weather alerts and visitor data management. In a significant proposed change to tourist transportation, the draft recommends that private cars, taxis and buses be stopped at designated green gateways located approximately 10 kilometres below fragile destinations. Beyond these gateways, movement would be restricted to electric or CNG vehicles, walking, ponies or cycles. The document proposes that electric vehicle fleets be operated by local youth cooperatives, self-help groups and registered local operators, while outside operators would not be licensed. Tangmarg has been identified as a possible green gateway for Gulmarg, Pahalgam town for Aru, Betaab Valley and Chandanwari, and Sonamarg market for the Thajiwas area. Emergency, defence, disaster-response and essential local-service vehicles would be exempted. The draft also proposes a Mountain Green Cess, with different rates for domestic and foreign visitors. According to its detailed tariff table, domestic tourists would be charged Rs 500 at Zone B destinations, including Gulmarg, Pahalgam, Patnitop, Sonamarg and Doodhpathri, and Rs 1,000 at Zone A sites such as glaciers, high-altitude lakes, alpine meadows and high-altitude trekking routes. For foreign nationals, the proposed cess is Rs 2,000 at both categories of destinations. It also proposes a freeze on new building permissions in glacier forelands, stream corridors and identified red zones during the initial implementation phase. Its overview section refers to a green cess of Rs 100 to Rs 300 per visitor per site, while the detailed tariff table proposes charges ranging from Rs 100 to Rs 2,000, depending on the category of visitor and destination. The difference would need clarification before the proposal is finalised. The recommendations, if approved and backed by the required legal and administrative measures, could significantly change how tourism, construction, transportation and environmental protection are managed in Jammu and Kashmir’s mountain regions.

stories.headline: Jhelum is calling
stories.title: Jhelum is calling
stories.summary: River Jhelum, which is considered to be the lifeline of Kashmir, has been facing extreme ecological threat due to unabated pollution, illegal mining and encroachments. Jhelum serves a dual purpose for Kashmir—its major source for drinking water and irrigation and importantly saves the Valley from floods. Ironically the river has been fast losing both these functions in absence of conservation measures. Jhelum originates from Verinag in south Kashmir, spans over 175 sq Kms and settles in Wular lake before flowing to Pakistan Occupied Kashmir (PoK) from Baramulla district in north Kashmir. The river is propelled by four streams—Sundran, Brang, Arapath and Lidder is Anantnag district. Besides small streams like Veshav and Rambiara also fed the river with fresh lease of waters. All water bodies flow into Jhelum making it an important part of Kashmir’s interconnected hydrological system. Despite its immense ecological importance, Jhelum is facing extreme pollution as all drains from south to north Kashmir directly flow into the river. The irony is that instead of constructing Sewage Treatment Plants, authorities have set up hundreds of pumping stations to empty drains into the river. The problem is compounded by dumping of solid waste and illegal sand mining. All these factors have severely affected flora and fauna and the hydrological system of the river. Jhelum has lost its carrying capacity also. It has been observed that the river swells and overflows after incessant rains for even 2-3 days. Wetlands like Hokersar, Bemina, Narakara, Batamaloo numbal, Rakh-e-arth, Anchar and Gilsar on the left and right of Jhelum, which acted as reservoirs of floodwaters, have been encroached upon, filled and converted into colonies. Deterioration of these wetlands have affected their capacity to absorb flood water—putting extra pressure on Jhelum. Jhelum Action Plan formulated for four towns of Anantnag, Srinagar, Sopore and Baramulla to intercept, divert, transmit sewage of these areas and treat it in STPs is still on paper. The intervention of the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir to restore the glory of Jhelum is timely. A division bench comprising Chief Justice Dr Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Yash Paul Bourney recently sought the report after Advocate Nadeem Qadiri, assisting as amicus curiae in the Public Interest Litigation (PIL) by Environmental Policy Group on conservation of Jhelum, raised concern over deteriorating condition of Jhelum. The Court has sought a report attesting to mining activities, proposed setting up of Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs) in river Jehlum as also construction or removal of embankments for flood control of the waterbody. It has also sought milestones achieved so far in the matter related to flood mitigation. EPG has filed the PIL in 2017 to flag the fragile flood management system in Kashmir and seek the court’s intervention for measures to protect Kashmir from future flood disasters. The PIL also highlights shortcomings in flood management due to which massive damage was caused during 2014 floods and seeks tangible steps to avoid such situations. EPG Convenor, Faiz Bakshi minces no words to raise red flags over illegal mining, untreated sewage discharge and condition of river embankments saying this has significant implications for the river’s ecological health, carrying capacity and flood-management system. EPG rightly states that these concerns cannot be addressed through administrative assurances alone and require transparent information, scientific assessment and effective implementation on the ground. Following incessant rains on September 7, 2014, Jhelum had crossed record 23-feet at Ram Munshi Bagh gauge, while level went over 36 feet at Sangam submerging localities on both sides of the river from south Kashmir to Srinagar. As per estimates flood water measuring about 120,000 cusecs surpassed the carrying capacity of Jhelum by five times. However no lessons have been learnt from the deluge. Despite the passage of 12 years, sustained and scientific measures are missing to increase the river’s carrying capacity. Believe it! Despite massive silt accumulation, no dredging has been undertaken in Jhelum in the last 5 years. On the other hand, unabated illegal mining in Jhelum’s tributaries —Doodh Ganga and Sukhnag has increased siltation in the river. An official report reveals that 15 lakh tonnes of riverbed material (RMB) comprising boulders, sand, nallah muck and gravel, were illegally extracted from Sukhnah river in the last several years. This wanton extraction of riverbed material severely altered the natural course of the river and extensively damaged its flora and fauna. Besides, imagine how many tons of silt must have been deposited in river Jhelum. The Ram Bagh flood spill channel looks like a forest with heavy growth of grass and other vegetation. Near Tengpora bridge, a vast chunk of the flood spill has been converted into a football ground. When water level in Jhelum rises, these bottlenecks hamper free flow of water. It is shocking to see how habitations have come up in the Jhelum’s floodplains. It was a practice of Dogra rulers to breach the Kandzal area to save Srinagar from floods. Excess water of Jhelum used to be diverted through Kandzal area and the waters would spread to Nowgam areas in central Kashmir Budgam areas. Now the Kandzal area is dotted with concrete constructions. The flood plains have been filled up! Earlier this year following incessant rains, Jhelum waters spread through its original flood plains from Shalina to Lasjan areas. The question is who allowed filling and constructions of Jhelum’s flood plains at the cost of endangering Srinagar city? Serious measures are missing to increase carrying capacity of Jhelum and restoration of its flood plains. We hope that judicial intervention will ensure long term conservation of Jhelum and restoration of its glory. And people shouldn’t forget that it’s also their responsibility to contribute their bit to protect their lifeline, the Jhelum. Author is Executive Editor, Greater Kashmir

stories.headline: Kerala High Court's Example Prompted Supreme Court To Strive For More Women Representation : CJI Surya Kant
stories.title: Kerala High Court's Example Prompted Supreme Court To Strive For More Women Representation : CJI Surya Kant
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant on Sunday (November 1) inaugurated the Platinum Jubilee Celebration of the Kerala High Court, marking 70 years since its inception on November 1, 1956.

"This High Court has been a place where constitutional promises have found practical meaning, where difficult questions of law have received thoughtful answers, and where successive generations have reposed their faith in the ideals of justice, fairness and dignity.
It is this legacy of public trust and constitutional commitment that makes today's occasion truly worthy of celebration..
I am, therefore, specially pleased that this historic occasion has finally brought me to this beautiful State," Justice Kant began his inaugural address.

"It seems to me that after I took over as Chief Justice of India, the collegium must have been influenced by this pragmatic and progressive approach of the Kerala High Court as we have been able to bring two distinguished women judges to Supreme Court in the recent time.

May be, somewhere behind the back of my mind, I must have been influenced with the visionary approach of this High Court where on judicial side, I was able to, not only pass an order, but persuade the majority of the State Bar Councils, the Bar Council of India and the District and High Court Bar Associations to ensure 30% representation for the women members of the bar.

All these historical steps find their strength and legacy somewhere and for that I will give full credit to the Kerala High Court because it was this High Court that at a time when the higher judiciary remained largely dominated by men or when the Bar Associations or the Bar Council were on the lighter side named as 'Men Club', I think the example set by this High Court has prompted and persuaded the Apex institution of this country to provide a formidable, fair and effective representation to the women members of the bar, whether it was a question of bench or the question of effective representation in Bar Council and Bar Associations."
Justice Kant also emphasised upon the High Courts' power to uphold constitutional and legal rights of the people, with a touch that can only provided by institutions closer to them.
He pointed to a 'new dimension of litigation' where litigants approach the Supreme Court for urgent listings before the High Courts.
He added that timely intervention and interim orders are often more important than final verdicts, and High Courts must strive to recognise the same.
"The Supreme Court, on its side, has consistently respected the institutional autonomy of the High Courts, including their authority to regulate their own rosters.
That position is rooted in respect for the constitutional status of the High Courts.
